title: Undersea Cables
objective: After this level you can explain how most internet traffic crosses the oceans through cables.
summary: Over 99% of data between continents travels as laser light in glass fibers inside undersea cables. Anchors and fishing, not sharks, cause most breaks.

cards.headline: Your video call to another continent almost certainly went under the sea.
cards.body: Not up to space. Undersea cables carry over 99% of the data that travels between continents, a figure the telecom research firm TeleGeography confirmed in 2023. So what is actually lying down there on the seabed?

cards.headline: Light inside a garden hose
cards.body: Modern undersea cables are fiber-optic. Lasers at one end flash light down glass fibers about as thin as a human hair, and receivers at the far end read the flashes. The fibers are wrapped in plastic and sometimes steel wire, and across the ocean the whole cable is typically about as wide as a garden hose. In the deep sea it simply lies on the ocean floor. Near shore it's buried under the seabed and given extra armor.

cards.fact: Ships' anchors are a bigger threat to the internet than sharks.
cards.context: Fishing vessels and dragged anchors cause about two-thirds of cable faults. Fish bites, sharks included, caused zero faults from 2007 to 2014, according to International Cable Protection Committee data. Breaks still happen, so countries use several cables and networks spread traffic across them. When one breaks, data keeps flowing over the others: Baran's idea from Level 62, a network that survives losing a piece.

mascot.line: Sharks get the blame, but anchors and fishing do the damage.

cards.headline: Why not satellites?
cards.body: Satellites are great for reaching places that aren't wired yet. But cables carry far more data at a fraction of the cost. Even your phone is wireless only as far as the nearest cell tower; from there, your data rides fiber. As of 2026, TeleGeography tracks more than 600 active and planned undersea cables, a web of glass laid across the ocean floor.

cards.headline: Undersea cables: surfaced
learned: Over 99% of data between continents travels by undersea cable
Lasers send light down hair-thin glass fibers in a garden-hose-wide cable
Fishing and anchors cause about two-thirds of faults; sharks, almost none
Traffic is spread across many cables, so one break doesn't stop it

questions.prompt: Inside an undersea internet cable, what actually carries the data?

options.label: Laser light flashing through hair-thin glass fibers
Electric current flowing through thick copper bars
options.rationale: Modern cables are fiber-optic: light, not current.

options.label: Radio waves bouncing along inside a hollow pipe
options.rationale: No radio here: it's light in glass fibers.

options.label: Seawater that conducts the signal from shore to shore
options.rationale: The signal travels inside the glass fibers.

questions.explanation: Lasers flash light down glass fibers about as thin as a human hair; receivers at the far end read the flashes.

questions.prompt: Why do cables, not satellites, carry almost all internet data between continents?

options.label: Satellites can't carry internet data of any kind
options.rationale: They can; they're great for places not yet wired.

options.label: Cables never get damaged on the ocean floor
options.rationale: Anchors and fishing break them regularly.

options.label: Cables carry far more data at a fraction of the cost
Laws ban satellites from carrying internet data
options.rationale: No ban: cables simply win on capacity and cost.

questions.explanation: Satellites help reach unwired places, but cables carry far more data far more cheaply.

questions.prompt: From Level 48: your phone talks by radio to the base station in its cell. How does your data usually travel on from that tower?

options.label: By radio again, hopping tower to tower overseas
options.rationale: Your phone is wireless only as far as the nearest tower.

options.label: Straight up to a satellite for every trip
options.rationale: Satellites mostly reach places not yet wired; cables carry far more.

options.label: As telegraph pulses on an old copper line
options.rationale: Modern long-distance links are fiber, not telegraph wire.

questions.explanation: A phone is wireless only to the nearest cell tower; from there your data rides fiber.
